message: For a quickly developed initial prototype, Elena, I can cover both the mechanical and electrical work without a problem. I do not expect the motors to need any metal mounting hardware because the proposed mounting approach should handle their torque easily. A 7-9 week timeline would be comfortable for me.

Stability will come from a solid base fitted with rubber/TPU feet, which should stop the unit from rattling or shifting. On the electronics side, the first build will stay as simple as possible and use off-the-shelf components. Selecting a motor that easily handles the liquid load should also make the mixing reliable. I could provide an initial BOM within 72-96 hours.

This approach and timeline sound great, Nolan, so let’s move forward.

The first step should cover:
• system layout
• motor + component selection
• basic wiring plan

From there, the goal is to get a working prototype running as quickly as possible and refine it afterward. Tell me what information you need from me to begin.

I’m ready to proceed whenever you are, Elena, and everything is prepared on my end. Before starting, I have one final question about power: should the unit plug into a standard 120v wall outlet, or would you prefer 12v power like a car battery? I’m ready to begin the CAD work and assemble the bill of materials, and I’ll promptly let you know if any other questions arise. Thank you—I look forward to working with you on the project.

For the initial version, let’s use a standard 120V wall outlet. Since it will be used at events, I want this version to remain as simple and reliable as possible; battery power can be explored later. Everything sounds good from my side, and I’m excited to begin. As you start the CAD and BOM, let me know what you need from me.

The selected setup works for me, Elena. I’ll implement 120v wall power while leaving open the option to adapt or change it to a 12v battery later if needed. I’ll start the CAD and BOM now, and as soon as you send the contract over, I can begin project work today. Looking forward to it!
The contract is being prepared now, and I’ll send it over next Friday once it is ready. I’m looking forward to working with you.
I appreciate it, Elena, and I’m looking forward to working with you as well.
Hello Nolan,
The contract has been included as an attachment.

I’ve reviewed the contract, Elena, and both the document and its terms look good to me. I agree to them. One important note: to make the arrangement official on upwork, you’ll need to submit it through their system using the hire button. The proposal I originally sent can be edited to include your milestones.
This is my first time hiring through Upwork, Nolan. Thanks for the guidance—I’m completing the process now.
I completely understand, so there’s no need to worry.

You can attach the contract, but the milestones should also be entered into the official upwork contract.

In the first section, you can add the PDF; in the following section, enter the milestones already written into the contract. My Upwork experience has only been as someone working for clients, not hiring them, so I’m not 100% certain what the process looks like from your side.
I'm completing the hiring process now.
I appreciate it, Elena. I’ll begin the work and keep you informed as it progresses.
Great! Thanks.

By next Thursday, I should have the initial BOM completed. After that, I’ll rough out the CAD, but final measurements and exact component placement cannot be determined until I physically receive the components.

One additional requirement came up later that I forgot to mention. In the attached image, the matcha mixer has no actual way to pour its contents. Please add a spout at the bottom, oriented toward the barista so pouring is easier.
Is the proposed approach feasible, or would another method work better?
Although it makes the design somewhat more complicated, the proposed approach should be feasible.
What makes the proposed spout more difficult?

Unless I’ve misunderstood, the motor is intended to sit beneath the bowl while the mixing head protrudes through its bottom. My current plan is therefore to place a hole directly in the bowl’s center for that mechanism. The drainage opening would need to be offset from the center hole, which may leave some liquid behind even after the bowl has fully drained.
Could we find a workaround that still keeps the process smooth and efficient?
Suppose we update the design to resemble this reference. A) Would that improve pouring efficiency? B) Would the build become simpler? C) Would the project timeframe change?

With this alternative design, pouring would be more efficient and the build would be simpler. The reason is that we would no longer need to manage possible leakage through a shaft seal, as the other method requires. Switching to this approach should not negatively affect the timeframe.

Let’s adopt this design while retaining the DJ Turntables vibe. The pour spot should face the baristas, all buttons need to be functional, and splashing should be minimized as much as possible. Keep the existing words on the machine unchanged, apart from the title, which should read "Elena's Chai Whisk," and use green accents. I also want to retain the thickness shown in the side view. The matcha wells should be deep, but the box itself must not become too large.

For V1, what simple, reliable implementation approach would you use for the spout? It must provide a smooth, controlled pour while remaining easy to clean between uses. A proper seal should prevent liquid from leaking into the base, and the open/close mechanism needs to operate cleanly without dripping.

Key Design Details

1\. Valve / flow control — I need a simple open/close valve or tap that prevents constant dripping and uncontrolled pouring.

2\. Seal at the bottom — This is critical: the bottom bowl seal must prevent external leaks as well as seepage into the electronics.

3\. Cleaning — Because matcha + milk leaves residue, the spout should either be removable or easy to flush and clean.

4\. Flow rate — I need a smooth, controlled stream rather than a slow drip or an explosive pour.

I’m reviewing everything here and will return shortly with a fresh design approach. Before that, I need to confirm one more design detail: how much matcha should each bowl mix at once? I’m currently considering 12qt bowls, which would support approx 11qt of matcha per bowl. Does that sound like the right capacity, or should I adjust it upward or downward?

Rather than increasing capacity to 12qt, I prefer the smaller bowls shown in the earlier design. Refilling is acceptable because the priorities are:
• better mixing quality
• consistent foam
• faster visual cycles during events

12 qt's would look like the attached picture, and bowls that large detract from the design and aesthetic. Let’s use a smaller bowl matching the size in the earlier pictures; I don’t mind refilling it.

With the smaller capacity, please make one additional adjustment: the bowls should be easy to remove and quick to swap. That will let me prepare bowls in advance and exchange them rapidly during events.
The bowl size shown here is acceptable. For the design color, though, I’d like to use beige.
understood.

Taking the recent design requirements into account, I’ve prepared the initial BOM for your review. Additional wires, hardware, and the custom-fabricated housing are not included yet, although I already have their materials in my shop; they will be added after the build begins. I’m now starting the initial cad design with rough component measurements. Once you approve and purchase the components, I can measure each physical piece accurately and fully refine the design. All components have been sourced from amazon so future changes or additions can be handled quickly.

For review, the component breakdown is as follows:

Vessels: 4.5-Quart Stainless Steel Bowls (Qty 2) - $21.18. These serve as the main mixing reservoirs. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00B4GTH0I>

Motors: 12V 450RPM Gear Motors (Qty 2) - $37.46. These are the high-speed mixing drive units. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B072R5QSRG>

Drivetrain: 1/2" Shaft Couplings (Qty 2) - $14.82. Each coupling links a motor to its extension shaft. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0D6XMSSFY>

Drivetrain: 1/2" x 14" 304 Stainless Steel Shafts (Qty 2) - $7.86. These extend from the motors to the whisks. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0DXPPL2LL>

Agitators: Wire Whisks (Qty 2) - $21.50. Their high-aeration heads provide mixing and frothing. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B078SL7D5L>

Control: PWM DC Speed Controllers (Qty 2) - $14.38. These give users independent control of vortex speed. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B09LS3ZWP9>

Power: 12V 35A DC Power Supply (Qty 1) - $10.49. This line provides the main power source for the electronics. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B08Y64DTK8>

Cooling: 80mm 12V Cooling Fans (Qty 2) - $15.98. The fans handle enclosure thermal management. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0FBFK9F4Y>

Structural: Brass Bulkhead Fittings 3/4" F to 1" M (Qty 2) - $9.16. These create through-bowl mounts for the drive shafts. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B09GVB9VLM>

Plumbing: 3/8" ID Silicone Tubing 18ft (Qty 1) - $7.15. This tubing forms the main transfer path from each bowl to its spigot. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B089YG7TWB>

Adapters: SS 3/8" Barb to 1" GHT Female (Qty 2) - $13.74. These adapt the spigot’s male threads to the tubing. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0GCDPCLNZ>

Coupling: 3/4" Barb Unions (Qty 2) - $4.49. The unions provide modular break points for cleaning. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0FH4FHV9Y>

Dispensing: Push-Style Beverage Spigots (Qty 2) - $7.50. These form the user-facing dispensing interface. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B08TVMD767>

Sealing: #5 Silicone Stopper 3/8" Hole (Qty 5) - $11.48. The friction-fit outlet seal prevents bowl leakage. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0DP43QKHG>

Connection: 3/8" Barb to 3/4" NPT Adapter (Qty 2) - $7.48. This creates a rigid interface through the stopper. Purchase link: <https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0DZPBSW8J>

The Estimated Component Total is $204.67.

Power for the electronics comes from a 120v-to-12v 35A DC supply, with each station using its own PWM speed controller. At each station, a 12v 450rpm motor connects through a 1/2" shaft coupling to a 1/2" stainless steel shaft, which drives the wire whisk for mixing and frothing the matcha. The electronics are actively cooled by 80mm fans. In the plumbing system, every 4.5 quart stainless steel bowl has a 3/8 barb outlet, where a #5 silicone stopper creates a press-fit, leak-proof connection. From the barb union inside that stopper, 3/8 silicone tubing runs to the 1" ght adapter, which threads directly onto the push-style beverage spigot.

Until I complete the initial CAD, some aspects will remain easier to understand in the finished model. I shared the expected materials beforehand so you can raise questions or suggest changes while I continue working on the design.
Hello, Nolan,

Because we are whisking a fine powder, the current whisk is too large. The selected bowls are 4.5qt, while those whisks are intended for 10qt bowls. We need to replace them with something smaller and thinner.

Could the spout be revised to match the diagram more closely? I’m unsure whether Matcha will retain the same consistency after running through the proposed spout, and it will not preserve the frothiness.
Here is the external product reference for the required whisk design: <https://www.amazon.com/Matcha-Reusable-Stirring-Japanese-Ceremony/dp/B0F3JBJ74L/ref=sr_1_22?s=home-garden&sr=1-22>
For the whisk we need, please follow the style shown in this reference. That type of whisk performs better with fine powder.

Regarding the whisk, understood—I’ll source a more suitable option for that component. The spout shown in your image is possible, but reproducing it would require us to rethink the design, develop custom circuitry, and do additional custom work. To make matcha flow through that type of spout on demand, we would essentially need a solenoid that opens and closes a valve inside the dispensing mechanism. Developing a reliable solution would involve custom mechanical parts, wiring, and some R&D, so it would likely push us beyond the timeline for this 1st edition. Several off-the-shelf spout alternatives are available, though. Could one of those work instead?
Here is the off-the-shelf beverage-spout search reference: <https://www.amazon.com/s?k=beverage+spout>
Greetings, Nolan,
Because dispensing the Matcha through a spout would make it lose its consistency, I don’t think that is the best approach. Could we create a gravity-based dispensing method instead?

Although this is a significant change to the engineering scope, I can make it work. I haven’t been able to find an off-the-shelf spout that closely matches the appearance of the one in your renders, but I did find an option that should function well. A solenoid valve would sit directly beneath the bowl, preventing any matcha from entering the spout until the button is pressed; releasing the button would stop the pour. Since no matcha would remain in either the spout or the tubing, its frothiness will be maintained. Please review this option: <https://www.amazon.com/Stainless-Pourers-BALTRE-Vinegar-Suitable> Alternatively, if keeping the appearance of the original rendered spout is more important, I could fabricate a custom version, though it would not be made from steel.

After giving it more thought and doing further research, I’ve revised my assessment: I believe I could fabricate the spouts from stainless steel myself while making them look quite similar to the rendering you supplied.

Go ahead with that approach, and please match the rendering as closely as possible; I really like both its appearance and functionality. I do want one change from the rendering: move the plate labeled "Elena's Chai Whisk" from the back of the machine to the front. The spout and mixers will face the baristas, while customers will view the machine from another angle, so the "Elena's Chai Whisk" plate needs to face the customer.
I’ll make those changes. Both the revised build strategy and the revamped BOM are nearly finished.
Ok.

To accommodate the new spout and solenoid valve, I’ve revised the original build plan while keeping its general approach. A stainless-steel bulkhead threads into the opening at the bottom of the bowl, and a stainless-steel nipple attached to it forms a quick-release mechanism so the bowls can be swapped easily. Sliding that nipple into the silicone plug creates a watertight seal. On the plug’s opposite side, a 3/4 inch 90 degree connector leads to the solenoid valve. Pressing the button will actuate that valve and dispense the matcha through the stainless-steel spout.

The exact whisks you previously showed me should be suitable for integration into the setup. Because they are roughly 3/4 the size of the wire whisk we originally planned, I expect them to work nicely with the 4.5qt bowls.
For review, here is the newly suggested BOM I’ve provided:
Could you send me a design mock-up showing the whisk you intend to use?

For the intended design, I would use the exact whisk you recommended yesterday from Amazon. I haven’t supplied the mock-up yet, but connecting that whisk to the steel mixing rod should only require a small, fairly simple adapter.

Hey Nolan — overall, the BOM is exactly the direction I was hoping for, and I really like it. Before we finalize anything, though, I’d like your input on a few details:

• Motors — could 450 RPM be too low for producing a strong, frothy matcha texture? Would increasing the speed make sense if we can still retain enough torque for smooth mixing?

• Whisk — in terms of consistency, durability, and foam quality, would a stainless-steel or milk-frother-style head perform better than the resin whisk?

• Spout — I want to keep the solenoid approach. For both texture and the overall visual experience, the pour needs to remain clean, controlled, and seamless: mix → open → pour.

• Splash / mess control — events make this especially important. The design should provide:
– minimal to no splashing during mixing
– a smooth, controlled spout flow without sputtering
– no dripping while the valve is closed
– effective sealing so liquid cannot leak into the base
– a splash guard or lip around the bowl if needed

• Cleaning — if possible, the bowls and spout components should either be removable or easy to clean.

Everything else looks great. What are your thoughts on these points, and would you adjust anything before we finalize the BOM?

On the motor question, I agree that more speed is appropriate, so I’ve selected replacements that spin at 1800RPM. The PWM controller will provide continuous adjustment from 0 RPM up to 1800 while preserving enough torque to mix the liquids.

Choosing the whisk is more difficult because few available options satisfy all of our requirements. We need a reasonably large mixing head so the entire bowl mixes consistently. The bowl is approximately 13 inch in diameter, whereas the plastic head currently listed on the BOM measures only about 3.6" diameter. By comparison, the original wire whisk I proposed was roughly 6.25" in diameter. Although that whisk is marketed for a 10qt bowl, I think it could still work well in our smaller bowl. A head resembling those on handheld electric frothers or mixers would probably be ideal, but those products are only available in very small sizes.

Splashing is not something I currently expect to be a problem. If the mixing becomes too rough, the motor speed can be adjusted during operation; should testing reveal splashing, we can also install the simple splash guard you suggested.

Cleaning has been considered as well. The bowl is already designed for very easy removal, and I also intend to make the custom spout removable so it can be cleaned easily.

Overall, we are nearly ready, and I’ll update the motor specification to 1800rpm. For the whisk, perhaps we should test 2 styles before choosing the best performer? It is one of the easiest components to exchange for a different design, and a simple adapter should allow us to attach virtually any whisk to the setup.

Another possible whisk has turned up on Amazon. It matches the resin whisk’s diameter but is made from stainless steel, and I could adapt it to the shaft after cutting off its handle: <https://www.amazon.com/Digead-Stainless-Versatile-Blending-Whisking/dp/B088TH4QDV>
The whisk works for me. For the motors, I propose setting the maximum speed at 2600—what do you think?
Yes, that works. Since the knobs can manually limit the operating speed, the extra capacity simply gives us more headroom to test and determine the right setting.
Great.

Because I’m having trouble locating a suitable motor in the 2600 range, I recommend using these 5200RPM motors instead. They will remain fully adjustable from 0 RPM to the 5200rpm maximum. Compared with the models suggested previously, these are slightly larger and should withstand extended use better; their shafts can also be shortened to the required length. <https://www.amazon.com/Motor-3000RPM-Output-Replacement-Electric/dp/B0GCZS9PVK>
Because the CAD work is still at a very early stage, the sharp angles and other provisional details will be refined later.

I’m good with this direction because the additional power and adjustable speed range make sense. The 5200 RPM motors work for me as long as we do not run them at maximum continuously; being able to dial them down for slow mixing or increase them for higher-speed frothing is ideal.

With that higher maximum, however, we need to ensure two things:
• splashing remains under control
• mixing stays smooth rather than becoming overly aggressive at higher speeds

If necessary, I’m open to adding a splash guard or adjusting the whisk position and bowl depth so the machine continues to operate cleanly. Overall, I approve this approach.
From the CAD images of the base, can you tell whether the whiskers will be removable?

Yes, the whiskers will be removable. The motor-mounting height is still being finalized, and it will probably need to be raised somewhat to leave enough clearance for removing the bowl and similar items.
Great.

For real event use, I want us to get several usability details right as the layout is refined:

• Bowl removal — the bowls should lift out easily, without being obstructed by either the whisk or the motor assembly.

• Whisk removal — because cleaning and swapping will be important during events, detaching the whisk should be quick and simple, preferably without tools.

• Whisk positioning — particularly across the higher RPM range, the height needs to support good foam quality while keeping splashing to a minimum.

• Splash control — the stronger motor must not make operation messy. Positioning, bowl geometry, or a subtle guard could be used if necessary to keep the system clean.

The overall design looks great; these are simply the practical details I want dialed in for actual events.

Before settling on the whisk position, I’ll test several heights and depths to determine which produces the most consistent and effective mixing. For the attachment itself, I’m currently considering a simple twist-lock design. Easy removal is essential because the installed whisk will directly block the bowl from being lifted out. Typical mixers handle that interference by allowing the mixing head to tilt upward.
Great.

Before we decide how to proceed, will you be sending an updated BOM? I also need to know how you prefer to handle payment for its parts. Should I purchase everything and forward it to you, or do the addresses connected to the product links automatically route the orders to you?
Either procurement option works for me, so choose whichever feels most comfortable and easiest on your end. In the meantime, I’ll prepare the revised BOM and send it over.

With your approval, I can handle purchasing the parts myself. Keeping them with me would make any necessary swaps a little easier, and you could reimburse the cost either through an added milestone or as a tip.
Finalized BOM:

While I’m reviewing the BOM, please hold off on buying anything. Having you purchase the parts and then reimbursing you will be more efficient, but the order should only be placed after I approve the materials.

Before I move ahead with ordering, Nolan, I’d like to confirm a few points. I’ve reviewed the finalized BOM, and everything looks very solid. I really like the direction and think we’re close to locking it in.

• Motor shaft — the listing describes an eccentric output shaft. Will that still provide smooth, centered whisk rotation, or would a straight or centered shaft offer better stability?

• Motor performance — moving to 5200 RPM provides useful flexibility, but can we adjust it precisely enough for smooth mixing without causing overly aggressive splashing at higher speeds?

• Solenoid flow — because the design uses on/off valves, will opening them produce a smooth pour, or could the liquid release too abruptly? The pour needs to remain clean, controlled, and free of splashing.

• Power supply — when both motors, the solenoids, and the fans are operating under load, will the 12V 35A power supply remain comfortably within its limits?

• Splash control — at the higher RPM, will the whisk position, bowl depth, and overall layout keep operation clean? For events, I want the system to be as splash-proof and mess-free as possible.

Everything not mentioned above looks great. Let me know your thoughts so we can fully resolve these items before placing the order.
One point still needs clarification: are you planning to fabricate the spouts yourself, as you mentioned earlier? I can’t find them listed on the BOM.

The motor’s eccentric-shaft description was carried over by mistake from the previously selected model; the new motor actually has a centered output shaft.

Flow through the solenoid should be smooth because the 3/4 outlet should keep liquids from releasing abruptly.

To reduce the risk of overheating or overloading, it would probably be wise to use a higher-output power supply. Higher-rated PWM controllers would also help reduce the overheating risk.

As for the spouts, they will be fabricated from 1/16 stainless steel. The material is listed at the very bottom of the BOM.
For greater power output, I’ll replace the parts we discussed with higher-rated alternatives.

The updated BOM is ready. Compared with the previous version, the component changes are limited to replacing the PWM motor controllers with higher-power models and swapping the AC/DC adapter for an 80A version. That adapter should provide more than enough power, including reserve capacity to keep anything from overheating. I also rechecked all current pricing and corrected the discrepancies between several listed prices and the prices now available.

Ordering can move forward from my side, provided one final point is confirmed: are the motor shafts, couplings, controllers, and power setup all fully compatible exactly as listed? Once you confirm that, please place the order, have every part shipped to you, and I’ll reimburse you.

Yes, Elena—the listed components have all been verified as fully compatible with one another. That includes the complete power system as well as the mechanical interfaces, such as the shafts and couplings.
Some progress has been made on the placard.
Now that the BOM is approved, place the orders and I’ll reimburse you.

Because the internal plumbing extends so far downward, the spouts will need to remain at the bottom. I had assumed the machine would sit at the edge of a table, but a platform would provide clearance as well. If you'd like, I can design the platform while I'm working on the enclosure.
